title: India-Pakistan Relations: Strategic Doctrines and Disputes

scenes.text: Why have India and Pakistan remained in conflict for over seventy years?
scenes.narration: Imagine two neighbours who share a long fence but cannot agree on peace. Why has normalising relations between India and Pakistan been so difficult for decades?

scenes.text: Feuding flat owners who block shared repairs out of deep mutual mistrust.
scenes.narration: As an everyday analogy, imagine two feuding members in a housing society. Neither trusts the other, so every simple repair turns into an endless, bitter courtroom fight.

scenes.name: Stephen P. Cohen
scenes.idea: India and Pakistan face a mutually hurting stalemate where neither can win.
scenes.narration: Scholar Stephen Cohen explains that this is a paired minority conflict. Neither side can decisively defeat the other, creating a mutually hurting stalemate that lasts for generations.

scenes.heading: Evolution of Indian Doctrines
scenes.narration: Past leaders tried peaceful engagement. Gujral offered unilateral concessions, and Manmohan Singh pushed trade, but Modi shifted track to isolate Pakistan and raise conflict stakes.

scenes.heading: Modi's Three Strategic Cards
items: Raise human rights violations in Baluchistan
Challenge Pakistan's claims on Gilgit Baltistan
scenes.narration: To counter proxy warfare, India started using three pressure cards. Modi highlighted human rights in Baluchistan, disputed Gilgit Baltistan, and reviewed water rights under the Indus treaty.

scenes.heading: Indus Water Sharing
scenes.narration: Under the Indus treaty, Pakistan receives eighty percent of the water from western rivers. India holds eastern rivers, but now insists blood and water cannot flow together.

scenes.heading: Territorial Border Disputes
items: Siachen boundary undemarcated beyond point NJ 9842
Operation Meghdoot secured strategic Saltoro heights
Sir Creek estuary disputed between boundary maps
scenes.narration: On the ground, borders remain unresolved. In 1984, Operation Meghdoot secured the icy Siachen heights, while the marshy Sir Creek estuary remains trapped between competing colonial maps.

items: Cohen describes a mutually hurting paired minority stalemate
Indian doctrines evolved from engagement to raising stakes
Siachen, Sir Creek, and Indus water remain key flashpoints
scenes.narration: Here is the lesson recap. First, structural mistrust fuels a stubborn stalemate. Second, doctrines shifted from dialogue to strategic pressure. Third, territorial and water disputes keep tensions high.
